shows.title: 2 Journeys
shows.description:
Married artists Gugger Petter and John Torrey share the gallery for a two-person show built around the written word. Petter weaves thousands of tightly rolled newspaper tubes into large-scale female portraits, a laborious technique that turns yesterday's headlines into something closer to tapestry or mosaic; the results nod to Renaissance portrait busts and Byzantine icons while staying rooted in the disposable material of daily news. Faces recur as studies and full compositions, including a piece inspired by the stray dogs of Izamal, Yucatán, that reads as a meditation on resilience as much as portraiture.

Torrey's contribution, the Lingua series, moves in a different register: oil paintings built from the shapes of Old Latin, Aramaic, and other ancient scripts encountered on his travels through Europe and the Middle East. Rendered as abstracted fields of mark-making, the letterforms sit halfway between language and pure pattern, so that looking at them becomes a kind of half-legible reading.

Paired together, the two bodies of work turn out to share more than a household — both artists treat text as raw material to be taken apart and rebuilt, one through collage-like accumulation, the other through paint. It's a quiet, well-matched two-hander from a gallery that has long supported mid-career Bay Area painters.

shows.title: Rising Tides
shows.dates_note: Venue does not publish an opening date; a closing party is listed for September 9, 2026, so the show is treated as running through that date.
shows.description:
Rising Tides is a benefit exhibition organized with the ocean-conservation nonprofit PangeaSeed, bringing together well over a hundred artists from the street-art, illustration, and gallery worlds around a single theme: the health of the sea. The work on view ranges from moody oil seascapes and gouache studies to spray-paint panels, ceramic sculpture, and mixed-media assemblage, with subjects spanning coral bleaching, plastic pollution, migratory fish, and mythic ocean figures like Yemaya.

Because the show doubles as a fundraiser, nearly every piece is for sale, and the checklist reads like a cross-section of contemporary muralists and pop-surrealists — Jessica Hess's photorealist gouache of a Bay Area coastline, George Rose's patterned leafy sea dragons, Natalie Gabriel's antique-framed panels, and dozens more, hung salon-style across 111 Minna's main gallery and bar areas.

It's less a curated survey than a communal outpouring, and that's the point: the sheer volume and variety of work is meant to demonstrate breadth of artistic concern for ocean ecosystems, with proceeds supporting PangeaSeed's public-art and advocacy programs. A closing party with music, sketching, and costumes wraps up the run on September 9.

shows.title: Abstract Objects of Devotion
shows.description:
Amy Trachtenberg's solo show at the David Ireland House grows directly out of her decades-long friendship and correspondence with Ireland, whom she first met in the late 1980s. Rather than treating the house as a neutral white cube, she works with it as a living collaborator, tucking folded and crumpled steel mesh and linen structures, bronze casts, silver pigment, ochre soil, and even human hair into the building's idiosyncratic corners and surfaces.

The exhibition also surfaces the material record of that long friendship: letters, postcards, aerogrammes, and collages exchanged between the two artists over the years become part of the installation, turning the show into something like a shared archive as much as a display of new sculpture. Trachtenberg calls the house "a refuge, a studio, a lab, a depot, an invitation, a magnet, a tuning fork, a plinth, a lookout, a lighthouse" — and the works are pitched at that same register of intimacy and multiple meanings, closer to concrete poetry arranged in space than to conventional object-making.

Trachtenberg's practice spans painting, collage, installation, and public commissions, with pieces held by BAMPFA, the San José Museum of Art, and the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, among others. Seeing her work installed inside Ireland's own former home and studio gives this show a rare charge: two ways of thinking about domestic space, material transformation, and duration talking directly to one another.

venue.name: 500 Capp Street Foundation (The David Ireland House)

shows.title: The Ringing in My Eyes
shows.description:
Andy Vogt builds his sculptures and site-responsive installations almost entirely from salvaged architectural material — wood lath, glass, and hardware pulled from Bay Area demolition sites over more than two decades. At the David Ireland House, he threads that reclaimed material through the building's intimate rooms and apertures, using mirrored surfaces, suspended linear structures, and concrete forms to catch and bend the light already moving through the house.

The effect is less an occupation of the space than a kind of careful listening to it: walls, doorways, and the traces David Ireland himself left behind become active participants rather than backdrop. Vogt's interventions are subtle by design, tuned to produce perceptual drift and a quiet sense of spatial memory rather than any single dramatic gesture.

Vogt has been developing this sculptural language of reclamation and reuse since the early 2000s, with major public commissions for San Francisco International Airport and Texas A&M University alongside gallery presentations at the Museum of Craft and Design, Southern Exposure, and SFMOMA's Artists Gallery. Showing alongside Amy Trachtenberg's Abstract Objects of Devotion, this exhibition rounds out a pairing of artists who each treat David Ireland's former home as an active, resonant material in its own right rather than a passive container for their work.

venue.name: 500 Capp Street Foundation (The David Ireland House)

shows.title: Sandow Birk: An Illustrated History of the Present
shows.description:
This is a thirty-five-year survey of Sandow Birk, spread across both of Catharine Clark Gallery's main spaces plus the media room, and it moves through nearly every medium he's worked in — painting, drawing, printmaking, ceramics, film. Birk has spent his career restaging the visual language of history painting around distinctly American, often bluntly political subject matter, and this show pulls threads from several of his best-known bodies of work, including In Smog and Thunder/War of the Californias, American Qur'an, and the Trumpagruel prints.

The anchor pieces are a pair of monumental 1992 graffiti collaborations with street artist REALM, Big Rat Trap and The Defence of the Many Food Market, both made in response to the 1992 Los Angeles uprising and recently revisited with new political interventions referencing ICE raids and current abuses of power. Birk builds these compositions by grafting his own conventional painting onto the structure of Jacques-Louis David's Revolutionary-era history paintings, then lets REALM's spray-painted imagery cut back across the surface — a genuinely odd and effective collision of eighteenth-century French painting, 1990s LA graffiti, and present-day politics.

Elsewhere, the show debuts new etchings from Birk's ongoing Trumpagruel series (a Rabelaisian send-up of the current president, made with Mullowney Printing in Portland) and includes Liberty on the Ruins of Democracy, a large new painting of Lady Liberty picking her way barefoot through an apocalyptic American tableau of abandoned cars, guns, and a ransacked convenience store. The whole exhibition is staged under the gallery's 35th-anniversary banner, tracing the through-line from the graffiti collaborations Catharine Clark first showed in the early 1990s to Birk's newest work — a useful lens for anyone wanting to see how one artist's satire of American power has evolved across three and a half decades.

shows.title: Open Net
shows.description:
Open Net turns Et al.'s main space over to programming rather than a fixed hang: a single painting per artist on the walls, a PA and modest stage set up in the middle of the room, and an open invitation for the public to book time for readings, performances, or workshops over the course of the month. The third gallery doubles as a viewing room for additional work and a green room for whoever is performing.

It's a loose, activated format rather than a curated exhibition in the usual sense — closer to the gallery handing over its keys for a month of experimentation than to a themed group show. Anyone interested in proposing an event can use the gallery's online booking system, and the roster of what actually happens fills in as the month goes on.

Paired with Punctum(s) in the front galleries, Open Net is the more open-ended, communal half of Et al.'s September program, built around participation and live activity rather than fixed objects.

shows.title: Punctum(s)
shows.artist: John Bankston, Jobi Bicos, Rebekah Goldstein, Bec Imrich, Nagi Lee, Quintessa Matranga, Steuart Pittman
shows.description:
Punctum(s) is a small, quietly considered group show built on the idea of proximity and distance — how a painting changes depending on whether you're pressed close to its surface, reading the grain of a mark, or stepped back far enough to see it as one small object on a field of white wall. Seven artists are hung across the front two galleries, each given room to hold their own wall before the works start to speak to each other as a loose chorus.

The artists span a real range of sensibility, from John Bankston's narrative figuration (shown courtesy of Rena Bransten Gallery) to Quintessa Matranga's and Nagi Lee's more intimate, small-scale paintings — Lee's Dangling, a modest oil on canvas, is a good example of the show's general pitch toward quiet, close-looking work rather than big statements. Steuart Pittman's contribution comes by way of Traywick Contemporary in Berkeley, adding another Bay Area through-line to the roster.

Curator Aaron Harbour frames the show around a lyric from Bill Callahan's song "Pigeon," using the image of a marriage — two people entering "the whole wide world" together — as a metaphor for how individual artistic practices join into community without losing their own footing. In the back room, works are hung a bit closer together, a shift in register the curator describes simply as "joyful together, just maybe."

shows.title: September Group Exhibition: Limbism
shows.description:
City Art's monthly rotating show is a members' salon: the co-op's roster of Bay Area artists each contribute new work, hung together salon-style rather than around a tight curatorial premise. This edition, promoted under the name "Limbism," continues the gallery's long-running format of a full-room turnover every month, timed to a First Friday-style opening reception.

Because City Art is an artist-run cooperative rather than a commercial gallery with a single dealer's eye, the September show tends toward variety — painting, photography, prints, and craft-based work sit side by side, reflecting the range of its membership rather than a single thesis. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about the working, unpretentious end of the Mission's gallery scene, where prices are accessible and the artists showing are often present in the room.

The opening reception falls on the gallery's regular First Friday slot, with the show remaining up through the end of the month.

shows.title: Drawn Together
shows.artist: Kevin Diep, Christina Marie Fong, Daniel Green, Nina Krietzman, Andrew Li, Steven Liu, James Miles, Cristina Saavedra, Ka Wai Shiu, Kate Thompson
shows.description:
Drawn Together, curated by Auriel Garza, is built around a simple observation: line is as much an emotional tool as a structural one. The show gathers works across marker, colored pencil, watercolor, and mixed media, all depicting people in groups — friends, families, teammates, bandmates, dancers — as a way of looking at how artists render connection and belonging through mark-making alone.

The range of approaches is part of the point. Steven Liu's loosely rendered marker crowds and James Miles's dense figure groupings sit alongside Kevin Diep's tightly rendered graphite-and-colored-pencil pop-culture scenes and Christina Marie Fong's mixed-media portraits on cardboard, giving the show a real spread of technique even as every piece returns to the same basic subject of people gathered together. Some works, like Daniel Green's colored-pencil rendering of The Rolling Stones, lean toward pop iconography; others stay close to home, in family kitchens or on the dance floor.

As with all of Creativity Explored's exhibitions, the artists are members of the studio's community of adult artists with developmental disabilities, and the show reflects the range of a program now in its fifth decade. It's a warm, unpretentious survey of a theme — togetherness, quite literally drawn — that plays to the strengths of line-driven, observational work.

shows.title: Automata Sigils
shows.artist: Billie Ocean, Kelley O'Leary, Sonya Rapoport, Ariella Robinson, Mia Weiner, and Carmen Winant
shows.description:
This group exhibition, co-curated by Janie Perez-Radler, gathers six artists whose work treats the body — and the marks it leaves — as a kind of divination tool. The show's title nods to the automaton and the sigil at once: art made through repetitive, semi-mechanical gesture that nonetheless carries private, talismanic meaning. Sonya Rapoport, the late Berkeley-based computer-art pioneer, anchors the historical end of that lineage, her data-driven works on paper putting an early, idiosyncratic spin on the idea of the body as a coded system.

Alongside her, younger and mid-career artists including Billie Ocean, Kelley O'Leary, Ariella Robinson, Mia Weiner, and Carmen Winant extend that inquiry into photography, textile, and sculptural forms, each treating pattern and repetition as a way of processing memory, ritual, and domestic labor. The installation photographs show a gallery hung salon-style with intimate, often modestly scaled works, suggesting a cumulative, diaristic reading rather than one built around single showstopper pieces.

Coming from a gallery best known for photography, Automata Sigils is a somewhat more expansive, cross-generational show, and it's worth seeing for the chance to encounter Rapoport's work in dialogue with artists who are clearly still metabolizing her example.
shows.reception: Saturday, June 27, 5–8 pm, curatorial walkthrough at 4:30 pm

shows.title: New & Recent Signs!
shows.description:
Lindsey White has spent years working signage into her photographs, sculptures, and installations, and this show turns that habit inside out: rather than photographing signs, she's made a room full of them. New & Recent Signs! collects the hand-painted, printed, and improvised placards she produced over the past year as functional pieces of other exhibitions and gatherings, now presented as freestanding works in their own right.

Stripped of the shows they were built to serve, the signs read as deadpan, funny, and slightly melancholy objects — the workaday scaffolding of an art career elevated to the main event. It's a light, confident gesture from an artist known for finding humor in institutional and vernacular language, and the installation views suggest a hang that's as much about typography and wit as it is about traditional composition.

For anyone who has followed White's photographic work, this is a chance to see the raw materials of her sensibility laid bare — proof that the jokes and observations that usually live in the margins of her images can carry a whole show.

shows.title: An Unending Path
shows.description:
Nicole White's An Unending Path is built around a single, specific piece of family history: a rural landscape in France that shaped the life of her great-uncle. Working across straight photography, printmaking, and proto-photographic processes like cyanotype and photogram, White treats that landscape less as a place to document than as a surface onto which time keeps getting written and rewritten.

The photographs favor mediated, layered views — windows shot through other windows, framed pictures caught inside larger frames — so that the act of looking is constantly interrupted and made visible. That doubling is the show's real subject: memory itself arrives filtered, partial, and a little degraded, and White's antique processes (with their long exposures, chemical stains, and soft edges) are a formal analogue for how the past actually reaches us. It's a quiet, patient body of work that rewards slow looking, and the artist talk on September 12 with critic Corey Keller is a good opportunity to hear White walk through her process directly.

For a gallery built around serious photographic practice, this is a strong, contemplative entry — less about spectacle than about the strange mechanics of inherited memory.
shows.reception: Artist Talk Saturday, Sep 12, 2026, 3-4pm, moderated by Corey Keller

shows.title: The Tramp
shows.artist: Caguiat Delacruz (Justin Caguiat and Rafael Delacruz)
shows.description:
Justin Caguiat and Rafael Delacruz's third collaborative project centers on a newly commissioned film starring a dog-walking, bowler-hatted wanderer modeled on Charlie Chaplin's silent-era Tramp — a fitting borrowed mask for two artists who trade paintings, drawings, and printing plates back and forth so freely that individual authorship starts to blur. The film follows its characters through Oakland streets and Half Moon Bay fields, but the real subject is close to home: San Francisco's own churn of displacement and reinvention, refracted through slapstick.

Rather than simply screening the film, the artists have turned the gallery itself into a set: deconstructed props and production furniture double as display fixtures, while storyboards, costumes, behind-the-scenes photos, and prints fill in the space around the projection. The effect is less a finished art object than an open rehearsal room, where the labor and improvisation behind the work are left visible rather than smoothed over.

It's Caguiat Delacruz's first institutional show on the West Coast, and a good showcase for the loose, collaborative, genre-crossing energy that has made their partnership distinct — equal parts homage, critique, and inside joke about what it takes to keep making art in a city that keeps changing under your feet.

venue.name: CCA Wattis Institute for Contemporary Arts

shows.title: RedSkyFalls
shows.description:
Alexandre Estrela's RedSkyFalls began as Portugal's pavilion at the 2026 Venice Biennale, a multi-part video installation that reacts in real time to seismic activity registered anywhere on earth. What the Wattis hosts is a satellite piece of that larger system: a "Réplica," an aluminum plate engraved with an animated creature — built from a composite of a fly's heartbeat, a fish larva's tail, a rat's whisker twitch — that flinches and freezes whenever the network detects a tremor somewhere on the planet.

It's a strange, quietly unsettling object considering its origin in incidental data: an artwork whose behavior is dictated entirely by forces outside the room, turning the gallery into a listening post for the planet's low-grade convulsions. San Francisco's own history with earthquakes makes it a pointed, apt host site among the piece's international network of venues, which also includes Los Angeles, Lima, Mexico City, and Lisbon.

Estrela has spent his career probing the seams between still and moving images, and RedSkyFalls extends that inquiry into something closer to a nervous system — proof that video art doesn't have to be looping or static to feel alive.

venue.name: CCA Wattis Institute for Contemporary Arts

shows.title: Reflections of Mani
shows.description:
British-born, Athens-based painter William Roper-Curzon built this body of work around repeated trips to Greece's Mani Peninsula, a rocky, sun-blasted stretch of the Peloponnese he's returned to again and again for its raw terrain and its sense of accumulated, half-buried history. The exhibition splits into two distinct working methods: smaller oil-on-board paintings made en plein air, directly on the exposed limestone and scrub, and larger studio canvases painted later from memory back in Athens.

That split gives the show its charge. The plein-air paintings are grounded and immediate, tracking the literal colors of olive groves, turquoise water, and sunburned hillsides; the studio paintings drift further from observation into saturated, almost hallucinatory color, letting memory and myth (Roper-Curzon nods to the classical geographer Pausanias's accounts of the region) reshape the landscape into something more psychological than topographical. Seen together, they form a kind of before-and-after of perception — the same place rendered first through the body, then through recollection.

Roper-Curzon is a colorist first, and the show's biggest pleasure is watching him push observed Mediterranean light into deliberately unnatural, jewel-toned territory without losing the landscape's specificity.
shows.reception: Artist Walk-through: Thursday, September 10, 5:30pm; Opening Reception: Thursday, September 10, 6-8pm

shows.title: 20 Years - Anniversary Exhibition
shows.description:
Eleanor Harwood Gallery marks two decades in business with a survey pulling together 21 artists from across its history, starting with Emily Prince, the very first artist the gallery showed when it opened in 2006. Rather than a straightforward greatest-hits hang, the show reads as a loose group portrait of the gallery's sensibility over time: the loaded, personal figuration of Lee Materazzi and Hunter Saxony III, the meticulous botanical sculpture of Tiffanie Turner, the landscape painting of James Chronister and Chris Russell, and the weaving-based work of Kira Dominguez Hultgren all sit alongside newer names like Carmen McNall and Joe Ferriso.

Anniversary shows like this one are as much about a gallery's identity as any single artist's, and the range on view here — from David Wilson's photography to Jill Sylvia's obsessively cut paper ledgers — makes the case that Eleanor Harwood's program has always been more about idiosyncratic craft and personal narrative than any single house style.

It's worth a visit both as a survey of two decades of Bay Area gallery history and as an unusually dense, varied hang in its own right.

shows.title: the antml:parameter>the passenger
shows.description:
Liam Everett's first solo show with Berggruen finds the Northern California painter working with a lighter hand than in past bodies of work, pulling back the thick gestural buildup that has defined much of his career. In its place: atmospheric fields of ink, oil, sand, and wood ash on linen, worked and reworked through erasure until what's left feels closer to residue than composition — traces of a process rather than a record of a single decisive mark.

The paintings grew out of Everett's reading on quantum biology and the relationship between light, photons, and living tissue, and that interest shows up less as illustration than as method: canvases laid flat on the studio floor absorb the literal conditions of sunlight over time, so each one registers something of the specific place and duration of its making. Titles like "Untitled (piezo effect)" and "Untitled (remote viewer)" gesture toward this quasi-scientific frame without pinning the images down to any single reading.

Everett, who trained in theater before turning to painting, treats the studio like a stage — moving around canvases with unconventional tools (a rusted trowel, a broken bean pole) in a physical process that extends into his garden as much as his studio. The result is abstraction that resists quick resolution: paintings meant to be returned to rather than settled on.
shows.reception: Thursday, September 10, 2026, artist discussion at 4:30pm followed by reception 5-7pm

shows.title: Defining the Century: Modern Visionaries from Picasso to Calder
shows.description:
This is a modern-masters survey drawn from the gallery's secondary-market holdings, gathering works on paper, paintings, and sculpture by ten of the twentieth century's defining European artists — Picasso, Braque, Gris, Kandinsky, Klee, Léger, Matisse, Miró, Tanguy, and Calder. Rather than tracing a single movement, the show sketches the century's break from academic tradition through a handful of representative gestures: a Calder standing mobile in painted sheet metal, a small Miró oil dense with his cosmic vocabulary, a Kandinsky board painting built from interlocking color fields, and a late Picasso interior scene.

It's the kind of exhibition blue-chip secondary-market galleries do well — an intimate, tightly hung survey rather than a loan-heavy museum retrospective, with pieces sized for a private collection rather than a museum wall. For a San Francisco audience, it's a rare chance to see small-scale, market-fresh examples by Picasso, Kandinsky, and Calder in the same room without a plane ticket.

Given the gallery's history — founder John Berggruen's father Heinz gave Matisse's cut-outs their first-ever exhibition in 1953 — the show also functions as something of a family footnote, tying the material on view back to a specific chapter of European modernism's dealer history.

shows.title: Richard Tuttle and Odili Donald Odita: Language and Pattern
shows.description:
Crown Point Press pairs two very different approaches to abstraction, both made in its own etching studio. Richard Tuttle's Type is a suite of 26 tiny color etchings — just three inches square each — printed with tarlatan chine collé, a technique that leaves a soft, fabric-like texture behind the ink. True to Tuttle's decades-long practice, the individual sheets are unassuming and almost casual, gaining their charge from repetition and installation rather than any single image.

Odili Donald Odita's contributions read as Tuttle's opposite: bold, hard-edged color-field etchings built from interlocking triangles and diagonals. The two-part Bliss and four-part Net series, along with two standalone prints, carry over the saturated geometric vocabulary Odita is known for in painting, translated here into the etching press's more physically constrained, additive process.

Seen together, the show becomes a study in how two printmakers can use the same medium and the same Bay Area workshop to arrive at opposite ends of abstraction — one dissolving form into near-nothing, the other building it up into insistent, jewel-toned pattern. It's a compact, smartly matched two-person show typical of Crown Point's print-focused program.

shows.title: Too Many Products
shows.dates_note: Site lists the show as "Extended through September 12th, 2026" with a closing reception that day; no original opening date is published. Gallery itself was closed for summer break August 25 – September 5, 2026, reopening before the closing reception.
shows.description:
Janet Delaney has spent decades photographing the everyday texture of American commerce and domestic life, and Too Many Products gathers color-saturated documentary work built around consumer culture — beauty salons, car interiors doubling as offices, cluttered counting-out of cash, and the small rituals of getting through a workday. The images have the loaded, slightly ironic color palette of 1980s American color documentary photography, in the lineage of William Eggleston and Stephen Shore, but Delaney's eye stays fixed on labor and commerce rather than pure landscape or roadside Americana.

Several images turn to more private terrain — a father in the bathtub, a hairstyle borrowed from Farrah Fawcett — suggesting the show is as much about the accumulation of domestic stuff and habit as it is about retail abundance. Delaney, a longtime chronicler of San Francisco's South of Market district and its displaced communities, brings the same clear-eyed, unsentimental attention here to the broader question of what it means to live surrounded by things.

The show's run was extended into September, closing out with a reception on September 12 — a good excuse to catch a compact but sharply observed body of work from one of the Bay Area's most consistent documentary photographers.

shows.title: Lee Friedlander: Maria
shows.description:
For nearly seventy years Lee Friedlander has trained his camera on his wife Maria, and this show gathers roughly fifty gelatin silver prints spanning the 1950s to the 2020s into what amounts to one of the longest sustained portraits in photography. It isn't a chronicle of posed intimacy so much as an accumulation of ordinary moments — Maria reading, driving, dozing in the sun, caught in a kitchen doorway in a checked dress — through which Friedlander's own restless formal habits keep surfacing: reflections, shadows, doubled and layered planes.

What makes the body of work distinct from a conventional marriage portrait is how little it flatters. Maria appears self-possessed and specific rather than idealized, her presence recorded with the same deadpan attention Friedlander has always brought to street signs, store windows, and self-portraits by shadow. In several images his own absence becomes part of the picture — an empty jacket on a doorknob, his shadow falling across her — turning the series into as much a portrait of the photographer's gaze as of its subject.

A new hardcover monograph accompanies the show. Given Friedlander's stature — a fixture of Szarkowski's 1967 New Documents alongside Arbus and Winogrand — Maria offers an unusually tender, long-view counterpoint to the wit and detachment more often associated with his street work.

shows.title: Bay Area Artists: Chromatic Narratives
shows.artist: Melissa Chandon, Matt Rogers, Deladier Almeida & Siddharth Parasnis
shows.description:
This group show brings together four Northern California painters who share a common ground — Wayne Thiebaud's influence, a love of high color, and subjects rooted in the everyday landscape — while pulling in different directions with it. Melissa Chandon reduces vacation-scapes (backyard pools, gas stations, red barns) to flattened, Pop-inflected geometry that one critic has compared to David Hockney's take on Northern California. Matt Rogers, a self-described disciple of Thiebaud, builds thickly textured floral abstractions where petals dissolve into rhythmic fields of oil paint.

Deladier Almeida contributes moody, atmospheric landscapes built from loose, breeze-blurred brushwork, while Siddharth Parasnis's paintings of boats and shoreline distill place into blocks of luminous, sharply angled color — a style he traces to influences from Edward Hopper's ambiance to Richard Diebenkorn's Bay Area color sense. Across all four painters, recognizable Northern California subject matter keeps giving way to color and structure as the real subject.

It's a tidy survey of how differently regional landscape painting can be handled once color takes precedence over description — useful viewing for anyone tracking the Bay Area's ongoing conversation with the legacy of Diebenkorn, Thiebaud, and the Bay Area Figurative painters.

shows.title: Overmuch
shows.description:
Terri Friedman's first solo show with Anthony Meier gathers a decade of woven work by the Bay Area artist and CCA professor, who came to the loom after seeing a monumental Miró tapestry in Barcelona. The pieces on view read as paintings built out of cotton, hemp, wool, chenille and metallic fiber — thick, saturated fields of color that oscillate between abstract textile object and pictorial image, including a new four-part series keyed to the light of the Bay at different times of day.

Friedman treats weaving as a slow, repetitive form of processing experience: several works here were made in the wake of her breast cancer treatment, including a large vitrine piece that folds the phrase "way 2 go" into a tangle of loosened, rope-like knots. The show's title, an old English word for abundance rather than excess, sums up the exhibition's mood — exuberant, plainly emotional color and texture standing in for the fullness (and difficulty) of being alive.

It's a good entry point into a strand of contemporary fiber art that treats the loom the way painters treat a canvas: as a surface for direct, physical, unhedged expression rather than craft for its own sake.

shows.title: Be Like the Sun
shows.description:
Rob Reynolds follows Terri Friedman into Anthony Meier's Mill Valley space this fall with a new body of work titled Be Like the Sun. Reynolds has long worked in a quietly literary vein of painting, pairing still-life and botanical imagery with an interest in books, writing, and the discipline of daily studio practice; the title suggests another chapter in that ongoing meditation on light, attention, and constancy.

Details on the specific works in the show are still emerging as the gallery finalizes installation, but the exhibition continues Anthony Meier's pattern of pairing serious mid-career painters with the intimate scale of its Mill Valley rooms. Worth a visit for anyone tracking contemporary California painting beyond the city's more crowded gallery districts.
